newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Doctors risk lives in rebel-held Albanian city.
newsitem.headline: Doctors risk lives in rebel-held Albanian city.

text.p: Hospital doctors risk their lives and work in filthy conditions to save victims of daily violence in this rebel-held Albanian city.

At Vlore hospital, where 52 violent deaths have been registered since Albania slid into near-anarchy earlier this year, doctors said they had regularly endangered themselves in their efforts to aid the wounded.
"People shoot guns in the hospital," said Maksi Qejvani, the 43-year-old duty officer.
"A lot of shooting is between gangs, who come here to protect their wounded," he added.
Walls inside the four-storey hospital are pockmarked with holes from bullets fired by grieving relatives of victims to pressure doctors to work harder to save lives.

Albania is awash with arms since armouries deserted by police and troops were looted following the failure of fraudulent savings schemes in which many had invested life savings. Nearly 300 people have been killed.
Doctors said Vlore hospital was desperately short of medicines and equipment and wards were not disinfected properly.
"We don't work in clean conditions. We lack equipment and antibiodics," said 53-year-old surgeon Zijadit Muhameti, who wore a dirty brown overcoat and peeling shoes.
The Geneva-based International Committee of the Red Cross ICRC) has made two deliveries of medicine to Vlore hospital in recent weeks, but it is still short of supplies, doctors said.
Despite the danger, doctors never miss their 12 hour shifts. "They come every time to work," Muhameti said. "No one has quit his job."

An Italian-led multinational mission is deploying across Albania to protect deliveries of emergency medicine and food to the poor. A first contingent of two dozen Italian troops arrived in Vlore on Thursday. Greek soldiers are due within days.
Patients at Vlore hospital said they were immensely grateful to doctors and nurses for helping them despite the risks to their own lives.

"I know it is dangerous for them, and I am very glad the doctors are working for us," said 22-year-old Ermir Caushi, who was caught in crossfire five days ago while out on a walk and hit in the stomach and arms.
He lay on a soiled, blood-soaked bed in a crowded ward, attended by cheerful doctors and nurses.
In another ward, Hasan Telati, 39, explained that he had been shot in the leg by gunmen who ambushed him and some friends as they patrolled their neighbourhood to protect their property.
"We were carrying guns. We had to defend ourselves," Telati, a welder, said.
Standing on crutches, he said doctors at Vlore hospital had looked after him. "They have treated us like gold," he said.
